data.title: TSX posts weekly gain as metal mining shares rally
data.description:
By Fergal Smith

Canada's main stock index rose on Friday, led by technology and metal mining shares, as investors weighed downbeat domestic jobs data that could reduce prospects of further tightening from the Bank of Canada.

The S&P/TSX Composite Index ended up 183.82 points, or 0.5%, at 35,789.09, after posting on Thursday its steepest drop in five months. For the week, the index was up 0.5%, after two straight weekly declines.

  • Huge Democrat gains in the US midterm elections this week led to investors anticipating increased scrutiny of the AI industry, triggering volatility in technology stocks and safe-haven demand for US Treasuries.

  • "What we saw post midterms was US Treasury yields came down, the US dollar weakened. That helped gold rebound," said Colin Cieszynski, chief market strategist at SIA Wealth Management. "It was a great week for mining."

  • The materials sector , which includes metal mining shares, rose 2.6%, lifting its weekly advance to 11.4%.

  • Canadian employment fell 4,700 in October and the jobless rate rose to a six-month high of 6.7%. It was the first jobs report since the Bank of Canada's recent move to raise interest rates for the first time in three years.

  • "It's a sign that the Canadian economy is not going gangbusters," Cieszynski said. "It's muddling along at best and so they're probably not under as much pressure to raise rates again."

  • Technology rose 1.8% as US tech stocks rebounded.

  • Energy added 0.2%. US crude oil futures settled 0.3% higher at $90.83 a barrel but were still posting a sharp weekly decline as investors weighed prospects of a de-escalation in the US-Israeli war on Iran.

  • Industrials (.GSPTTIN) were a drag, falling 0.9%, and heavily weighted financials ended 0.2% lower.

  • Shares of Trisura Group tumbled 29.9% after the specialty insurer's quarterly results missed estimates.

data.title: As tech swoon roils market, US inflation data on tap
data.description:
Key points:
  • CPI data on Tuesday, with markets expecting rate hike in December
  • CoreWeave, Applied Materials, Cisco highlight tech earnings
  • US stocks slammed amid data-center slowdown worries after midterms

By Lewis Krauskopf

Jolted investors head into next week with the US stock market on shaky ground, as deep selling in the pivotal AI trade creates unease ahead of the release of inflation data and earnings reports from several technology companies.

Stocks were slammed on Thursday by concerns that widespread victories by Democrats in Tuesday's US midterm elections would slow the AI data-center buildout. That fed anxiety about a trade that has been at the heart of the market's rally this year.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite closed Thursday nearly 12% below its October 6 all-time high, exceeding the 10% threshold that confirms a correction. That and other major losses for equity indexes reversed the previous session's gains in the immediate aftermath of Tuesday's midterm elections, in which Democrats routed President Donald Trump's Republicans and won control of the US Congress.

Tech stocks led a modest rebound on Friday, but the major indexes still posted weekly losses.

With volatility rising, tests for the market arrive next week. On Tuesday, the government will release the monthly consumer price index report, perhaps the most closely watched inflation measure. Earnings reports are due from tech companies CoreWeave , Applied Materials and Cisco Systems .

"It is a fragile momentum trade," said Marvin Loh, senior global macro strategist at State Street. "You have got this regulatory, political party overhang, which I think is going to stay with us until we really get a sense of how significant of a slowdown we're thinking about."

VOLATILITY SPIKES AFTER MIDTERM RESULTS

Stocks endured severe swings in the wake of Tuesday's midterms. In addition to winning control of the US Congress, Democrats also won several key governors' races in data-center-heavy states such as Texas. Public backlash about environmental and other concerns over the spread of data centers was a prominent issue in the midterms.

Sharp gains on Wednesday in major equity indexes were accompanied by a slide in oil prices. That gave way on Thursday to steep equity declines, when the Cboe Volatility Index also hit a seven-month high.

Selling was widespread on Thursday — with all S&P 500 sectors ending lower — but it was most acute among AI and tech stocks. The S&P 500 tech sector sank 7.3%, while the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index tumbled over 12% — both posting their biggest one-day drops in more than six years.

Major indexes were still logging gains for the year, with the benchmark S&P 500 CBOE:SPX up nearly 8% in 2026.

"There are a lot of cross-currents and narratives right now that people are trying to grapple with in the wake of the (election) results," said Garrett Melson, portfolio strategist with Natixis Investment Managers Solutions.

CPI TESTS DECEMBER RATE-HIKE BETS

The CPI report for October comes as investors are expecting the Fed to raise rates in December to fight inflation. The US central bank held steady last month after hiking in September for the first time in three years.

As the market swooned on Thursday, traders pulled back modestly on rate-hike bets. But following a strong jobs report on Friday, Fed fund futures were suggesting a roughly 80% chance the central bank hikes at its December 8 to 9 meeting, according to LSEG data.

Investors also will focus on the CPI report for clues to the Fed's rate path into 2027, with about two more standard 25-basis-point increases expected in total for this cycle.

"If you get a hot number and then you start adding additional tightening because the inflationary environment looks like it's accelerating, that's just something else that investors would have to absorb," Loh said.

After a busy slate of corporate results, the schedule calms next week. Several reports could be consequential for the tech and AI trade, including CoreWeave, the cloud company at the center of concerns about financing the AI buildout. Its shares have been pummeled in recent weeks.

"If they do have a little bit more of a cautiously optimistic view in terms of being able to find ways to get projects across the finish line, that I think helps to kind of alleviate some of these concerns," said Natixis' Melson.

Tech was underperforming the S&P 500 over the past month by its largest amount since May 2002, Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Advisory Services, said in a note on Thursday.

"We are now seeing something of a buyers’ strike in tech," Lerner said.

data.title: Bipartisan US Senate bill could speed up AI data center buildout: report
data.description:
A U.S. Senate bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was introduced in late September, could fast-track the permitting process of infrastructure needed to power data centers.

Although recently introduced, the Senate might move a vote forward as soon as next week, according to The Verge.

The Bipartisan Policy Center said the White House has been involved and wants the bill to move while Republicans still control the House and Senate, according to the report. If it passes, U.S. President Donald Trump plans to sign the bill into law before the end of the year.

The bill was introduced by Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT) and Martin Heinrich (D-NM). The 400-plus-page bill would make procedural changes to the National Environmental Policy Act. NEPA requires federal agencies to consider the environmental impact of various federal actions, such as permitting, leasing, federal funding and federal projects.

"Those reviews take too long, cost more than they should, and can be undone years after they are finished," according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. "BAAJA rewrites the statute's procedural provisions along three lines: scope of review (what agencies must analyze), which projects get reviewed at all, and how long the process takes."

The bill seeks to simplify the process for the approval and development of high-voltage transmission corridors. It addresses specifics of the National Historic Preservation Act, which can add years to the timeline of projects before construction even begins.

Regarding data centers, the BAAJA requires operators of data centers with 20MW or more of capacity to be required to cover all additional expenses and not pass those off to other customers.

"These provisions aim to build transmission faster while giving states and consumers a stronger voice in how lines, especially those triggered by data centers, are approved and paid for," the BPC said.

In addition, the bill would prompt the U.S. Energy Information Administration to update its Form 861 to begin separating out electricity use by data centers for AI, cloud computing and cryptocurrency mining.

"Whether it is permits to bulldoze wetlands, the fast-tracking of gas pipelines or general environmental review, with this legislation, data centers would not need to answer to the concerns of local communities," said Christy Goldfuss, executive director of the Natural Resources Defense Council, according to the report. "People would be shocked to realize their representatives are rushing such a consequential decision."

U.S. citizens' concerns over data centers were front and center in the midterm elections on Tuesday. An AP poll found that 56% of voters surveyed said data centers were a "crucial or major" factor in their vote.

data.title: Yue (Justin) Tang Proposes Buyout of X Financial with 47.97% Stake
data.description:
Yue (Justin) Tang Proposes Buyout of X Financial with 47.97% Stake

Yue (Justin) Tang reported beneficial ownership of 47.97% of X Financial and disclosed that Mangrove Coast Investment Limited proposed buying the shares it does not already own. The proposal, submitted to X Financial’s board on November 6, 2026, offers $6.03 in cash per American depositary share, or $1.005 per ordinary share. The preliminary offer could take X Financial private and remove its American depositary shares from the New York Stock Exchange, but it does not commit either side to complete a deal.

Investor Intent

Mangrove’s preliminary, non-binding proposal seeks to acquire all X Financial ordinary shares it does not beneficially own. Mangrove expects to fund the purchase with a mix of equity from Mangrove and its affiliates, including cash or rolled-over equity, and loans from financial institutions.

The parties still need to negotiate and sign final agreements, and neither side has to complete the proposed transaction. If they do complete it, X Financial’s American depositary shares would become eligible for deregistration and delisting from the New York Stock Exchange.

Investor's Background

Yue (Justin) Tang is a Malta citizen and serves as X Financial’s chairman and chief executive officer. He is the settlor of the Mangrove Coast Trust, whose beneficiaries include Tang and his family, and he serves as the sole director of Mangrove Coast Investment Limited. The trust owns Mangrove, an investment-holding company incorporated in the British Virgin Islands.

data.title: Lululemon Appoints Two Key Executives Amid Leadership Shakeup
data.description:
By Natalie Weger

Lululemon Athletica appointed two new key executives as Chief Executive Heidi O'Neill rounds out her leadership team to help address slumping sales at the athleisure company.

The company on Friday said it has appointed Ben Hallam as chief brand officer and Emily Sunderland as chief strategy officer, effective Nov. 9 and Nov. 23, respectively

Hallam, who succeeds Nikki Neuburger, most recently served as the senior vice president of marketing at Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts.

Sunderland was a managing director and partner at Boston Consulting Group, succeeding Rachel Acheson.

O'Neill, a former Nike executive, has already made several executive changes since she took the helm of the company in September. Last month, she brought on the former head of Gap's Athleta brand as president and chief product officer, and also tapped a former Walmart executive as chief operating officer.

Lululemon said it's still looking for a chief technology officer and chief communications officer.

data.title: IPOs Struggle in Tech Selloff. Berkshire Has a Winner. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Andrew Bary

The old investment adage to avoid initial public offerings has held up this year, as many stocks are trading well below their IPO prices.

Barron's looked at 18 companies that made their U.S. stock-market debuts in 2026, including marquee offerings like SpaceX, Cerebras Systems, Innio, Madison Air Solutions and Jersey Mike's, found that 15 of them are below their offering prices. Many are down 50% or more.

SK Hynix, already public in South Korea, made its U.S. debut in July through an offering of American depositary shares. That stock also is trading below its U.S. offering price in July.

Why do IPOs often falter? Companies that come public often are in hot industries, and carry high valuations to reflect investor optimism. That enthusiasm often wanes, however. This year, some deals were keyed off the AI buildout and enthusiasm for that trend has faded.

There are some winners, notably Arxis, a defense contractor with an aerospace focus; Pershing Square, Bill Ackman's investment management company, and Bending Spoons, the rollup of mature tech companies like AOL.

Give Berkshire Hathaway some credit. The company headed now by CEO Greg Abel picked the right deal when it invested $600 million in Bending Spoons at the July IPO at $29 a share. The stock traded recently at $45, up 55%. In October, Berkshire bought another $330 million of stock at $33.

Berkshire rarely buys IPOs — reflecting former CEO Warren Buffett's well-founded aversion to them. It participated in Snowflake's IPO in 2020.

Looking at some of the larger deals, SpaceX trades around $131, against an IPO price of $135; Cerebras at $82, less than half its IPO price of $185; and SK Hynix at $124, versus its U.S. offering price of $149.

One of the better ways to play IPOs in a diversified way is through the Renaissance IPO ETF. It adds newly public companies every three months as part of a regular rebalancing and companies cycle out after three years. Individual holdings are capped at a 10% weighting at rebalancing.

Its largest holdings now are SpaceX at nearly 10%, followed by SK Hynix and Astera Labs, both at more than 7%. The ETF, now around $45, is off about 2% so far this year.

Be careful about SK Hynix ADRs. While chip stocks have come under pressure, SK Hynix's U.S. shares trade at a big premium to the Korean shares that Barron's estimates is close to 50%.

Busted IPOs also can be a good place to look for values, and there are many companies to comb through this year.
